title: Redwood edgecases demo - long context & high TPS (streaming/timeouts)
summary: AE/SE demo of Redwood platform focusing on edge cases: 100k token contexts, sustained high TPS, streaming backpressure and timeout behavior. Customer has strict PCI-like constraints, prefers VPC/private deployment but open to dedicated reserved capacity. Agreed next steps: send pricing, run a small benchmark pilot, share SOC2/KMS docs.
next_steps: Sofia Ramirez - send pricing and reserved capacity options
Ethan Cole - share benchmark harness and suggested test plan
Acme to confirm pilot dataset and SLA targets
Schedule technical PoC kickoff the week of 2026-08-10

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-29
Time: 14:00 PT
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Ramirez (Redwood AE), Ethan Cole (Redwood SE), Maya Lin (Redwood Product), Raj Patel (Acme Head of ML), Olivia Chen (Acme Platform), Marcus Lee (Acme CTO)

[00:00] Sofia: Hey everyone thanks for joining, we should be all set. quick agenda: show how Redwood handles long contexts, talk about high TPS patterns and streaming - especially backpressure and timeouts, then Q&A and next steps.
[00:18] Raj: cool yeah we really care about two things: long context for chargeback and reconciliations, and sustaining high TPS for realtime fraud scoring. also, security - we run in a VPC, strict KMS and audit logs.
[00:35] Ethan: great; quick intro from me, i'm Ethan on the SE side, i'll demo api and console flows and show optimize recommendations. couple of caveats in the demo are synthetic but reflect real load.
[00:48] Olivia: one note, our current infra is a mix of managed endpoints and some in-house GPUs. we hit a lot of tail latency occasionally when context spikes.
[00:58] Maya: also want to call out we support quantized models and prefix KV cashing - sorry KV cache i always say cashing - to reduce token cost.
[01:08] Marcus: (laughs) all right KV cache noted.

[01:25] Ethan: jumping in - i'll share my screen. first i'm hitting the Redwood console, route is set up for hosted API and we also show a dedicated cluster. here is a side-by-side: hosted for quick launch, dedicated for steady high TPS, private for VPC/on-prem.
[01:48] Ethan: demo doc link: https://redwood.ai/demo/edgecases (note: placeholder link)
[02:05] Ethan: first long context - we're pushing a 100k token ledger history into the prompt to simulate reconciliation. backend will stream token generation. as you'll see latencies depend on model variant and KV cache hits.
[02:30] Raj: can you remind us how you handle sequence sharding or attention optimizations? we saw memory blow up in our POC with other runtimes.
[02:39] Ethan: good q - runtime selects kernel paths based on architecture and sequence length, it uses attention tiling and streaming chunking. for really long contexts we rely on prefix KV caching and chunked attention to avoid O(n^2) blowup. sometimes you still see stalls while KV is being materialized.
[02:59] Olivia: and does that materialization happen on the GPU or host?
[03:05] Ethan: mostly on GPU memory; we page in KV pages and if it spills we fall back to host pinned memory which adds latency. that's one reason we recommend dedicated capacity for predictable throughput.

[03:30] [05:00] Ethan: initiating the 100k token run - streaming enabled.
[05:05] Speaker 4: um the stream looks fine here, but there's a chunk where tokens stop for ~3s. i think that's the KV materialization you mentioned.
[05:20] Ethan: right. that pause is expected in heavy long-context workloads when cache warmup occurs. we have prefetch heuristics in Optimize that suggest pre-warming or batching smaller prefixes to avoid that.
[05:42] Raj: if prefetching helps, what about cost? prefetch seems like extra tokens.
[05:49] Maya: tradeoff - prefetch adds token cost but reduces tail latency and retries. Optimize will quantify expected cost delta per 1k requests.

[06:10] Ethan: next demo - sustained high TPS. we configured a traffic generator to hit 1,200 TPS sustained across 8 routes, mixed short and medium contexts.
[06:24] Olivia: that's about our target in peak hours. we also have bursts up to 5k TPS but short lived.
[06:32] Ethan: okay launching. backend is set to dedicated pool with auto-scaling but a capped burst.
[06:45] [09:00] Speaker 2: we're seeing an increase in latency percentiles after a couple minutes, 95th jumps from 80ms to 400ms.
[09:15] Ethan: that's the backpressure kicking in - when the runtime's request queue grows, we prioritize shorter requests and apply flow-control. streaming responses may be delayed and client timeouts can be triggered.
[09:34] Raj: how do you recommend clients handle streaming backpressure? we have a 30s client-side timeout.
[09:42] Ethan: several patterns: 1) move critical paths to dedicated reserved capacity to avoid queueing; 2) enable streaming with small chunk sizes and client-side incremental rendering so partials are useful; 3) implement graceful retries with idempotency keys and checkpointing of partial KV offsets. also set client timeouts slightly above expected p95 under load.
[10:08] Olivia: checkpointing sounds heavy. any SDK support?
[10:13] Ethan: we have SDK helpers for resumable streaming and idempotency tokens in our JavaScript and Go clients.

[10:30] [12:10] Ethan: now i'll intentionally reduce allowed max inflight on the pool to simulate stricter resource limits - to show timeouts and fallbacks.
[12:25] [13:00] Speaker 4: stream stalled and then the server returned a 524-ish timeout. transcript shows 'gateway timed out'.
[13:10] Ethan: yes in hosted scenarios we return standard http status codes for timeouts; we also emit a rich error payload with model_state and suggested remediation: retry, reduce context size, or route to a cheaper model variant.
[13:30] Maya: the console also surfaces SLO breaches and the exact token window where the timeout happened.

[13:50] Raj: what about retries for side-effecting operations? our scoring service writes to a ledger so we can't double-score.
[13:58] Ethan: must use idempotency keys and transaction tokens. our server can attach a deterministic request UID and you can store offset in your own db. we discourage blind retries on side-effecting API calls.

[14:20] Marcus: security: SAML SSO and KMS - can we run private with our KMS and HSM?
[14:28] Sofia: yes private deployments support customer-managed KMS and HSM integration and we surface audit logs. we are SOC2 Type II compliant; i'll send the certs and artifact pack.
[14:40] Raj: do you support VPC peering or private endpoints?
[14:45] Ethan: both; private control plane + VPC peering and an on-prem package for disconnected environments.

[15:00] [19:00] Olivia: on telemetry - how granular are cost/latency breakdowns? we need token-level cost per route.
[19:08] Maya: Console shows per-route, per-model token breakdowns, cost by token category (prompt/completion), and latency histograms. Optimize provides suggestions like quantize-to-int8 for embeddings-heavy routes.

[19:40] Raj: any known gotchas with quantization and long contexts? we saw hallucination increase in other runs.
[19:48] Ethan: quantization can slightly change model behavior; Optimize recommends eval prompt sets and A/B canaries; we integrate with eval harness so you can track quality regressions.

[20:10] [25:00] Ethan: quick Q: if we hit backpressure and shed load, do we prefer graceful degradation or full failure?
[25:12] Sofia: Redwood supports policy-level routing: degrade to a cheaper model variant, return partial streaming output, or fail-fast based on route policy. you can configure fallback rules in the console.

[25:45] Raj: demo was helpful - one more: can you show a pilot plan for our case?
[25:52] Ethan: propose 3-week pilot: week 1 - ingest sample prompts and run baseline latency/cost; week 2 - run sustained TPS benchmark and measure tail; week 3 - run private/dedicated comparison and finalize SLA targets.
[26:10] Olivia: timeline wise we want a production decision by end of sept.

[26:30] [30:00] Sofia: okay quick recap and next steps - we'll send pricing, SOC2/KMS docs, benchmark harness and draft pilot plan. schedule PoC kickoff and we'll loop in infra.
[30:45] Marcus: curious about pricing on reserved capacity vs hosted during bursts.
[30:52] Sofia: reserved gives predictable unit costs and headroom; hosted is pay-as-you-go but can have higher per-token unit cost for sustained loads. we'll include a model of expected spend in the pricing sheet.

[31:20] [40:00] Raj: last q - client SDKs and timeouts defaults, what should we tune?
[40:10] Ethan: by default sdk timeout is 30s; for streaming long contexts bump to 90s, and set chunk_size smaller if you need partial renders. we'll include recommended SDK settings in the docs.

[41:00] Olivia: any limitations in checkout for 100k token contexts? memory wise?
[41:08] Ethan: if you need >100k we recommend model sharding and pre-compiled kernel paths; we can propose an architecture review in the PoC.

[41:40] [55:00] Sofia: ok thanks all. i've captured action items. we'll follow up in email with attachments.
[55:10] Raj: thanks team, that was helpful.
[55:20] Marcus: appreciate the demo.
[55:25] Sofia: bye everyone.

End of transcript. Notes: small transcription glitches (KV cashing, gateway 524-ish) and occasional speaker attribution errors are present.
